transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-04
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~55 minutes
Attendees: Lena Park (Redwood AE), Marco Diaz (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Mercury Search - Head of Search), Tom Becker (Mercury - ML Engineer), Sara Liu (CTO)

Summary (auto-gen, noisy): deep dive on embeddings + reranking perf and cost, vector dims, batch size tradeoffs, quantization effects, VPC/on-prem considerations, next steps to run benchmarks and pilot dedicated capacity

Topics: embeddings vector dims (128/256/512), reranker latency SLOs, batching and queueing, KV cache usefulness for rerank, quantization accuracy vs perf, private deployment constraints

Transcript:
00:00:02 Lena Park: hey everyone thanks for joining, um we'll do a deep dive today focused on embeddings and reranking perf and cost, marco will run through the numbers and then we'll get into specifics, priya maybe quick intro from your side
00:00:15 Priya Nair: yeah hi thanks lena, i'm priya, head of search at mercury, our main goal is to reduce end-to-end query latency for our product search, target P95 is 150ms today but we want to get down to ~80-100ms for reranked results, budget sensitive so cost per q matters
00:00:32 Tom Becker: and hi i'm tom, i run the ml infra, our current stack is elastic for indexing, pinecone for vector store, a small transformer reranker (6-layer) running on our k8s fleet, we get vari- we have noisy tail latencies and high cost on peak
00:00:47 Marco Diaz: cool thanks, just to set expectations we'll cover embedding encode time, vector dims tradeoffs, reranker model latencies, batching strategies and how Redwood handles batching and KV cache, then quantization options and on-prem/VPC notes

00:01:10 Marco Diaz: quick number baseline - these are representative: embedding generation for a typical 512-token doc chunk using our embedder (256d) is ~6-12ms on our hosted CPU path or 2-4ms on GPU optimized path, for 128d vectors it's even faster ~1.5-3ms, so vector dim directly affects encode time and index size
00:01:35 Priya Nair: sorry quick q, when you say 256d is 6-12ms that's for batch size one encode?
00:01:42 Marco Diaz: yeah batch size one, single request latency. If you batch encodes (we do continuous batching), you can get amortized per-item time down but you introduce queueing delay so depends on qps distribution

00:02:05 Marco Diaz: on the retrieval side - assuming an ANN index like HNSW - recall/latency tradeoffs are mostly orthogonal to model dim but index size grows with dims, so 512d vectors mean roughly 2x the index memory over 256d. That increases cost for memory and also I/O when paging parts of the graph for large corpora
00:02:29 Tom Becker: we currently store ~200M passage vectors, memory is already a constraint, curious about quantization here - can we go int8 or 4-bit and keep accuracy?
00:02:40 Marco Diaz: good q - quantization has evolved. int8 often gives small drop (<1-2% in most ranking metrics) for float32->int8 with proper calibration. 4-bit/INT4 or LLAMA-style 4-bit quantization can give larger accuracy hits on embeddings - more pronounced for reranking if the reranker takes raw embeddings. For retrieval-only vector stores, product teams often accept int8 or PQ (product quantization) to reduce memory by ~4x, but for reranking (dense cross-encoder) we usually prefer keeping the reranker at higher precision while quantizing the ANN index

00:03:12 Priya Nair: when you say reranker at higher precision, do you mean the cross-encoder model runs unquantized on GPU?
00:03:20 Marco Diaz: yes, typically the reranker/cross-encoder runs at fp16 or int8 on GPU for inference. Redwood's runtime supports int8 kernels for transformer attention which gives 1.5-2x perf uplift vs fp16 on many setups with minimal accuracy loss, whereas aggressive 4-bit can save more cost but requires validation

00:03:45 Lena Park: also wanted to call out KV cache - it's more often discussed for generation but there are some wins for rerank workloads, marco?
00:03:53 Marco Diaz: yeah so KV cache is mainly about avoiding recomputation when the same prefix or tokens are used repeatedly. For pure rerank (cross-encoder) it's less impactful than for autoregressive generation, but in scenarios where the query or context has repeated segments across requests (e.g., session-based re-ranking), KV caching reduces compute. Additionally, for prefix caching we can cache embedding encodes for common queries which reduces encode latency at the retrieval stage

00:04:20 Tom Becker: let's talk throughput numbers - what qps can we expect for a 6-layer reranker at 512d inputs on a single GPU?
00:04:27 Marco Diaz: ballpark: a small 6-layer cross-encoder at 512-d inputs (depending on tokenization) can do ~200-600 qps with batching on an A10/A100-class GPU when heavily batched. Single-request P95 might be 20-60ms when running fp16 and low batch sizes; with int8 kernels and optimized kernels we often see P95 down to 15-30ms in dedicated runtime. But remember that's model-only; total E2E includes retrieval and encoding and network hops
00:04:58 Priya Nair: our SLO is P95 <=100ms for the whole pipeline; what are the realistic knobs?
00:05:05 Marco Diaz: knobs: 1) vector dim reduction (e.g., 512->256) reduces index size and embed time, small accuracy tradeoff; 2) use a lightweight bi-encoder for candidate scoring and run cross-encoder only on top-k (k=10-50) - this is common; 3) increase batch sizes for GPU throughput but accept queueing delay; 4) quantization (int8) for reranker and index; 5) dedicated capacity to avoid noisy neighbors and get predictable latency

00:05:35 Tom Becker: i like bi-encoder + cross-encoder cascade, that's our current pattern, we run cross-encoder on top-20, but the cost at peak kills us. Curious what Redwood's cost math looks like for dedicated vs hosted per qps for that setup
00:05:47 Lena Park: we provided an example cost calc in the deck - roughly, dedicated capacity for a single GPU pool with autoscale has a base cost but reduces per-q token cost vs pure hosted for heavy sustained traffic. Marco, can you summarize the pilot pricing we mentioned?
00:05:58 Marco Diaz: sure, rough example: assume cross-encoder at 6-layer running fp16 on a single A10 -> sustained throughput ~300 qps with batching; cost put in ballpark $X/hr for GPU (we'll send exact in sheet). For hosted bursty workloads, the per-query cost can be 2-4x higher due to multitenancy and on-demand resources; dedicated gives you predictable perf and reduced per-unit cost if usage is sustained. We'll send a worked spreadsheet

00:06:30 Priya Nair: ok please include a worked example for bi-encoder (256d) + cross-encoder (6-layer 512 tokens) with k=20 and with/without int8 quantization so we can see cost/latency/metric tradeoffs
00:06:43 Marco Diaz: will do

00:06:50 Marco Diaz: let's dig into batching/queueing math quickly - we measure two components: service time (model inference) and queueing delay. At low qps, batch size is one and you get low latency but poor GPU utilization. As qps rises, we accumulate requests into batches (say target batch sizes 32/64), throughput increases (tokens/sec) but per-request latency increases due to the batch wait time. Redwood's runtime uses adaptive batching with latency SLO-aware thresholds so batches form only up to a max wait of X ms depending on SLO. That gives a nice middle ground: high throughput while meeting P95 latency budgets
00:07:25 Tom Becker: what's X ms in practice?
00:07:28 Marco Diaz: default is 10-30ms depending on model and SLO class; for strict low-latency SLOs we set lower max-wait, for cost-sensitive workloads we allow a higher max-wait to increase batch sizes. We'll expose that as a config you can tune per-route

00:07:45 Priya Nair: curious about tail latency - we get big tails during cold-starts and when autoscaling kicks in, how does Redwood handle cold vs hot pools?
00:07:54 Marco Diaz: we have warm-pool options for dedicated and pre-warmed instances for hosted. Also automatic fallback to smaller model variants during overload to maintain a response (graceful degradation). For private deployments e.g., VPC or on-prem we can run warm pools as well but customer's infra will determine the exact cold-start timings. We also offer autoscale burst policies and can pin capacity for critical routes
00:08:18 Sara Liu: any specifics on VPC/on-prem networking - our security team will insist on no egress to public networks for embeddings in some countries
00:08:26 Lena Park: redwood private supports a private control plane + on-prem package, we integrate with customer KMS/HSM for key management, and no egress is possible if you run the inference plane fully on-prem. We'll schedule a security deep-dive
00:08:39 Marco Diaz: technical note - if you're doing on-prem and want HNSW graph access across GPUs, you need a fast network (RDMA recommended) to avoid graph-fetch bottlenecks. Also if using NVMe-backed index shards ensure we benchmark page-in latencies
00:08:56 Tom Becker: good to know, we have 100Gbps between nodes so should be fine but will validate
00:09:02 Marco Diaz: another point on caching: prefix and embedding caches really help for query hot-keys; the runtime exposes TTLs and a cache warming API. For reranking, caching the bi-encoder embeddings and candidate IDs reduces the cross-encoder load. We also have an intelligent prefetcher for session traffic
00:09:22 Priya Nair: ok let's talk about accuracy vs quantization - do you have A/B data for int8 vs fp16 on our reranker? we saw small quality drops in some evals
00:09:33 Marco Diaz: we ran internal evals on common re-rank datasets - int8 with per-channel quantization on attention weights typically shows <1% drop in nDCG@10 compared to fp16 for our 6-layer reranker. 4-bit needs careful tuning, and in some ranking-sensitive queries we saw 2-4% drop. We'll provide the eval spreadsheets but recommend testing on your corpus
00:09:55 Priya Nair: thanks - we'll need the test harness so we can run on our metrics
00:10:00 Marco Diaz: yep will share the eval harness and the script to run locally or on Redwood pilot
00:10:07 Lena Park: let's go through an example scenario end-to-end with numbers - priya can you confirm expected peak qps and target P95?
00:10:15 Priya Nair: peak 900 qps sustained for 10-20 minutes during campaigns, average 150 qps. P95 target 100ms, P99 ideally under 250ms
00:10:26 Marco Diaz: ok, rough design: use 256d bi-encoder for retrieval (fast encodes, small index), maintain 512d cross-encoder for final scoring but only on top-20 candidates. If cross-encoder at fp16 yields model P95 ~25-40ms per request (with batching), plus retrieval + encode 10-30ms, you land around 50-80ms E2E at high throughput if batching is tuned. For 900 qps sustained you'll want a small GPU pool (2-4 GPUs depending on batching and model), dedicated for predictability. We'll dimension in the follow-up spreadsheet
00:11:04 Tom Becker: what about cold-cache scenarios where none of the queries are in prefix cache? that will spike retrieval costs and index IO
00:11:11 Marco Diaz: yes cold cache means extra IO; you can mitigate with more RAM for index or use warmed replicas. Also Redwood's routing can send queries to regionally-localized replicas to reduce cross-region latency. For on-prem we recommend allocating enough memory to keep hot shards resident
00:11:27 Priya Nair: any notes about model compilation/kernel selection? we sometimes see different perf on AWS vs on-prem GPUs
00:11:34 Marco Diaz: runtime compiles kernels based on model arch, sequence length, and hardware. We select optimized attention kernels (e.g., flash attention) when supported; that gives big perf wins. For GPUs older than Ampere or in some vendor setups we fallback to more generic kernels; that's why we benchmark per target infra. We'll include A100/A10/T4 numbers in the sheet
00:11:55 Lena Park: okay let's surface some risk areas - priya do you have any compliance or data residency constraints we should be aware of?
00:12:02 Priya Nair: yes EU customer data must remain in EU for EU-configured products, some customers require logs not be retained beyond 30 days, and we need SOC2-type audit info
00:12:13 Marco Diaz: Redwood supports per-tenant data retention policies, audit logs, and encryption with customer-managed keys. For EU data residency we can run inference in EU regions or on-prem; we'll include the compliance checklist
00:12:25 Sara Liu: we'll definitely want to see SOC2 and the VPC deployment diagram
00:12:29 Lena Park: we'll send those
00:12:34 Marco Diaz: quick perf note about batch sizes for cross-encoder: we usually try slots of 16-64; beyond that the per-request queue wait gets large. For your SLO of P95<=100ms with 900 qps, i'd recommend target batch size 32 with adaptive max-wait 12ms as a starting point
00:12:55 Tom Becker: what's the memory footprint per GPU for the reranker model at 512 tokens and fp16?
00:13:02 Marco Diaz: rough: a 6-layer cross-encoder with 512 token input in fp16 is ~6-8GB including KV and activations if you use attention optimizations; int8 reduces model memory but also impacts perf. Add buffer for batching and workspace, plan 12-16GB per GPU for safe operations
00:13:20 Priya Nair: that helps, thank you
00:13:30 Marco Diaz: i want to call out two deployment patterns we've seen: 1) Dedicated inference pool for reranker + shared retrieval layer (ANN) in a separate memory-optimized cluster; 2) co-located on same GPU cluster for small teams. Pattern 1 helps with predictable latency and easier index scaling
00:13:49 Lena Park: and for pilot we usually recommend pattern 1 to get realistic perf/cost numbers
00:13:56 Priya Nair: are there any recommended test corpora or benchmark scripts?
00:14:01 Marco Diaz: yes we'll share our benchmark harness: sample harness does QPS sweeps, measures P50/P95/P99, measures nDCG changes under quantization and different dims, and collects GPU utilization and index memory metrics. It also simulates cold cache vs warmed cache runs
00:14:20 Tom Becker: can your harness run on our k8s cluster or does it require Redwood infra?
00:14:26 Marco Diaz: both - we provide a local runner that can hit your infra or we can run in Redwood pilot. The harness emits a CSV/Sheets link for analysis
00:14:35 Priya Nair: ok next - fallback/graceful degradation strategies?
00:14:39 Marco Diaz: three common fallbacks: 1) model variant fallback (use a smaller reranker when under load), 2) candidate cap reduction (reduce k from 20->10), 3) degrade to bi-encoder only. Redwood's routing can apply these rules automatically based on latency or capacity signals
00:15:00 Priya Nair: seeming good; can you summarize the recommended starting config for pilot?
00:15:04 Marco Diaz: recommended starter: bi-encoder 256d for retrieval, index using HNSW with int8 PQ, cross-encoder 6-layer fp16 with optional int8, k=20, batch target 32, adaptive max-wait 12ms, dedicated pool of 3 x A10 (we'll size exactly in spreadsheet). Pilot length 2-4 weeks to gather real traffic and cold/warm patterns
00:15:30 Lena Park: great, last part - operational/observability - what dashboards do you want to see?
00:15:37 Marco Diaz: we'll enable per-route P50/P95/P99, batch sizes, queue wait times, GPU utilization, index memory and page-in rates, cache hit ratios, and inference errors. Also a rerank quality guardrail: run periodic evals against a labelled set and alert on nDCG regressions
00:15:58 Priya Nair: that will cover our needs, thanks
00:16:03 Lena Park: ok let's recap next steps
00:16:06 Lena Park: recap: 1) Marco runs rerank benchmarks for 256/512 dims + quant variants and shares spreadsheet; 2) Lena sends pilot pricing and security docs; 3) Priya shares qps distribution and some labeled eval sets; 4) schedule security deep-dive if on-prem needed
00:16:26 Priya Nair: yep that's correct, i'll share labeled set and traffic profile by Friday
00:16:32 Tom Becker: we'll validate network perf and share any infra limits
00:16:35 Lena Park: perfect, thanks everyone
00:16:40 Marco Diaz: thanks all, one small noise note: the transcript may have small recognition errors, will follow up in docs
00:16:50 [meeting ends]
